accepted.question_text: For a fixed integer m >= 1, define f(t) = 1/(e^{-mt}; e^{-2mt})_infty and define coefficients C_{m,n} by sum_{n>=0} C_{m,n} q^n = 1/(q^m; q^{2m})_infty, where (a; q)_infty := product_{j>=0} (1-a q^j). Can one obtain a local expansion of f(t) as t -> 0^+, beyond the leading bound and leading asymptotic term, so that one gets a full asymptotic expansion for the coefficients C_{m,n} rather than only the leading-term asymptotic?

evidence.quote: One can show by a calculation similar to that of [9, Proposition 2.1] that: f (t) ~ 1/sqrt(2) e^{pi^2/(24mt)}, as t -> 0+. We leave this to future work.

This remains the major obstacle for this family, as one would like to have a full asymptotic expansion in addition to the leading term. It is likely that this could be done by using Mellin transforms (as in [1]) but this remains an open problem.
To obtain the asymptotic formula, we need a local expansion near t = 0, which remains an open problem.

accepted.question_text: For integers m >= 1, let C_{m,n} be defined by sum_{n>=0} C_{m,n} q^n = 1/(q^m; q^{2m})_infty, where (a; q)_infty := product_{j>=0} (1-a q^j). The paper proves that for integers m, k >= 1, one has C_{m,n} congruent to 0 modulo m whenever n is congruent to one of 0, 1, ..., k-1 modulo k. Can one prove congruences for the family C_{m,n} for all moduli, and not only for the moduli covered by those residue-class congruences?

evidence.quote: Theorem 1.2. For m, k >= 1, C_{m,n} satisfies the congruence: C_{m,n} == 0 (mod m), if n == 0, . . . , k - 1 (mod k).
It would be interesting to use the method of Ahlgren and Andersen to obtain congruences for the family C_{m,n} (and possibly D_{m,n}) for all moduli.

accepted.question_text: For integers m >= 1, let C_{m,n} be defined by sum_{n>=0} C_{m,n} q^n = 1/(q^m; q^{2m})_infty, where (a; q)_infty := product_{j>=0} (1-a q^j). The paper proves that for integers m, k >= 1, one has C_{m,n} congruent to 0 modulo m whenever n is congruent to one of 0, 1, ..., k-1 modulo k. Are there other families of generating functions, beyond the family defining C_{m,n}, that satisfy this same congruence-vanishing pattern on the first k residue classes modulo k?

evidence.quote: Theorem 1.2. For m, k >= 1, C_{m,n} satisfies the congruence: C_{m,n} == 0 (mod m), if n == 0, . . . , k - 1 (mod k).
We leave open the question as to whether there are other families of generating functions which have the congruence property described in Theorem 1.2.

accepted.question_text: Fix an integer k >= 1 and distinct integers r and s between 1 and k, and define coefficients G_k(r, s)_n by sum_{n>=0} G_k(r, s)_n q^n = 1/((q^r; q^k)_infty (q^s; q^k)_infty), where (a; q)_infty := product_{j>=0} (1-a q^j). When r + s is congruent to 0 modulo k, the paper gives congruences modulo m for residue classes n congruent to 0, 1, ..., k-1 modulo k in the cases m congruent to 0 modulo k and m congruent to -1 modulo k. Can one obtain broader congruence results for these G_k(r, s) families, and are there other generating functions of the form G_k(r, s) that exhibit the same congruence behavior?

evidence.quote: Remark. The congruence properties in Theorem 1.3 and 1.4 can be extended to other families. For instance, define: sum_{n=0}^infty G_k(r, s)_n q^n := 1/((q^r; q^k)_infty (q^s; q^k)_infty), where r and s are distinct integers between 1 and k.

Then the proof can be adapted to show that: G_k(r, s)_n == 0 (mod m), if n == 0, 1, . . . , k - 1 (mod k), r + s == 0 (mod k), m == 0 (mod k). and: G_k(r, s)_n == 0 (mod m), if n == 0, 1, . . . , k - 1 (mod k), r + s == 0 (mod k), m == -1 (mod k).
However, it would be interesting to obtain congruences for these families.
We leave open the question as to whether there are other types of generating functions which can be written as G_k(r, s), which also exhibit the congruence behavior described in Theorem 1.3 and 1.4.

It remains an open question as to whether congruences for all moduli exist in the D_{m,n} family. This remains open.
